questions.prompt: Rania is building the glossary at the back of her notebook: one word of the theme on the left, one definition on the right. She has reached the word "drought". Which definition must she copy beside it?

options.text: the amount of rain that falls on a place in a year
the slow using up of something until little of it is left
a long period during which little or no rain falls
the act of leaving waste somewhere it should not be left

questions.explanation: "a long period during which little or no rain falls" is the definition of a drought: the word names a stretch of time without rain, which is why a country speaks of three years of drought and not of three millimetres of drought. "the amount of rain that falls on a place in a year" defines rainfall, a quantity that is measured; a drought is what happens when that quantity stays too low for too long, so the two words are the cause and its measure, not the same thing. "the slow using up of something until little of it is left" defines depletion, the word your book uses for the ozone layer; it applies to a resource that is being consumed, not to the weather. And "the act of leaving waste somewhere it should not be left" defines the verb to dump, which belongs to pollution and has nothing to do with rain.

questions.prompt: In lesson 27 you matched four adverbs with four degrees: high, moderate, excessive and sufficient. Your teacher rubs the table off the board and asks for one line back: which of these four adverbs names a MODERATE degree, that is, a real amount but less than a high one?

options.text: quite
very
too
enough

questions.explanation: "quite" is the adverb of moderate degree: "The result is quite good" says the result is good, but stops short of saying it is good to a high degree. "very" is exactly that high degree, one step above; writing very where the meaning is moderate makes a claim your facts may not carry. "too" names an excessive degree: it does not say a lot, it says more than anybody wants, which turns a description into a complaint. And "enough" names a sufficient degree, the level that is needed and no more; it is also the one adverb of the four that stands after the adjective, as in wide enough, and never before it.

questions.prompt: A report on the repair of a village well near El Kef contains this line: "The old pump was light enough for two men to carry to the new site." A pupil has to report what that line says about moving the pump. Which reading is right?

options.text: It stayed where it was, because it was too light.
Two men tried to carry it and could not.
The line says how heavy the pump was, not whether two men could move it.
Two men were able to carry it to the new site.

questions.explanation: "Two men were able to carry it to the new site." is what the line reports. Adjective + enough + to says that nothing stood in the way of the action: the weight of the pump was under the limit, so the carrying was open to them, and the words for two men name the people the lightness was enough for. "The line says how heavy the pump was, not whether two men could move it." is the commonest misreading: enough looks like a plain measurement, but the structure exists precisely to say what that measurement allows, and here it names the two men it allows it to. "Two men tried to carry it and could not." turns the sentence into its opposite; failure is what too + adjective + to reports, as in too heavy to carry. And "It stayed where it was, because it was too light." invents a reason the line does not give, and uses too where nothing excessive is described.

questions.prompt: Emna is writing one line for her club's poster about a new water filter. She has two things to say about it, and she wants both to count: the filter is cheap, and it is easy to fit. Which line is correctly built?

options.text: The filter is not only cheap but also it is easy to fit.
The filter is not only cheap but also easy to fit.
Not only the filter is cheap but also easy to fit.
The filter is not only cheap but easy to fit also.

questions.explanation: "The filter is not only cheap but also easy to fit." is the correct line: not only and but also join two members of the same grammatical kind, and here both members are adjectives, cheap on one side and easy to fit on the other. "The filter is not only cheap but also it is easy to fit." breaks that law by putting an adjective on the first side and a whole clause, with its own subject and verb, on the second. "Not only the filter is cheap but also easy to fit." joins two members that are no longer of the same kind: the filter is cheap is a whole clause, and easy to fit is an adjective. And once not only carries a whole clause like that, English wants the auxiliary in front of the subject, as in Not only is the filter cheap, but it is also easy to fit. And "The filter is not only cheap but easy to fit also." splits the pair: also belongs immediately after but, or round a following subject, never at the end of the sentence like an afterthought.

questions.prompt: After a school concert in Sousse, Wassim says he liked what the singer was saying, word for word. His sister Rania says she did not catch a single word, but she has been humming the line of notes all evening. Which line reports the two of them?

options.text: Wassim liked the melody, and Rania liked the lyrics.
Wassim liked the tunes, and Rania liked the compact disc.
Wassim liked the lyrics, and Rania liked the melody.
Wassim liked the melody, and Rania liked the tunes.

questions.explanation: "Wassim liked the lyrics, and Rania liked the melody." is the right pair: the lyrics are the words that are sung, which is what Wassim followed word for word, and the melody is the line of notes, which is what Rania hummed without catching a word. "Wassim liked the melody, and Rania liked the lyrics." has the two words the right way round for each other but the wrong way round for the two people, and gives Rania the words she says she missed. "Wassim liked the melody, and Rania liked the tunes." names the music twice, since tunes are melodies in the plural, and so says nothing at all about the words Wassim heard. And "Wassim liked the tunes, and Rania liked the compact disc." ends on the object a recording is stored on, which is not something anybody can hum after a live concert.
